parakeet: Here's the paradox. Christianity often claims to be grounded in truth and to stand against idols or falsehoods. Yet Jesus, Santa, and the Easter bunny often share the same stage in Christian households. In families where Jesus is central, the other magical figures nearly always show up. In households where Jesus isn't central, these myths are often absent. It's almost as if Jesus, Santa, and the Easter Bunny are members of the same category, benevolent mediaries who all enforce a moral or cultural script through magical presence. This makes the religion's anti-idol stance ring extremely hollow. If truth is the anchor, why tolerate and even encourage so much make-believe alongside it? Especially in American Christianity, there is a heavy reliance on intermediaries. Why? Christianity absorbed these myths from European folklore and American consumer culture. They became seasonal anchors for family and community celebration. Myths work to soften the harshness of doctrine. A child who fears hellfire can also look forward to Santa's gift, the bunny's candy, or the fairy's coins. Fear is paired with sweetness, creating a carrot and a stick system. These myths create mental pathways for accepting unseen systems. If a child can trust that their tooth will be exchanged for money by an unseen being, it's not a big leap to accept that their prayers are being heard by an unseen God.
